learning_outcomes.description: Be able to plan, develop and carry out an independent research project.
Obtain an in-depth knowledge of the specific topic area through a thorough literature review.
Develop research skills and be able to locate and use information sources.
Present results of research in a written thesis.
Present results of research in an oral seminar.

assessments.task_description:
At the end of the course, each student will submit a written thesis and subsequently undertake an oral examination.

The thesis is due by 5:00 pm on Monday of the first week of the examination period. The oral examination must be held after submission of the thesis and before the end of the examination period. The exact date and time should be arranged by the student in consultation with the supervisor, and the two additional examiners: a subject-matter expert and a non-specialist examiner.

Written thesis

The thesis should introduce the project and explain its motivation and the broader context of the research field. It should demonstrate familiarity with the relevant literature. The literature review submitted halfway through the year will likely provide the basis for this part of the thesis.

The description of the project should be sufficiently detailed to allow a new student to understand how the work was conducted and, where appropriate, reproduce it using the information provided. The thesis must clearly identify which aspects of the project were completed by the student.

The research results should be presented clearly and interpreted critically. The student should explain how the findings relate to the current state of research in the area. The conclusion may also discuss possible extensions of the project and directions for future work.

The expected length of the thesis is approximately 25 pages. This is a guideline rather than a strict requirement. Heavily theoretical theses may be shorter, whereas experimental theses containing many plots or substantial amounts of data may be longer. Conciseness and clarity are valued by the assessors, and a densely written thesis may communicate the required material in fewer pages.

A physics thesis template is available and may be used in preparing the thesis.

Students are strongly encouraged to submit a draft of the thesis to their supervisor or supervisors for feedback well before the submission deadline.

Students who believe that they may be unable to submit the thesis by the deadline because of extenuating circumstances should contact both their supervisor or supervisors and the course coordinator as soon as the circumstances become apparent.

assessments.task_description:
Each student will undertake an individual oral examination after submitting the written thesis.

The oral examination complement the written thesis by providing an authentic assessment of the student’s understanding of, and intellectual contribution to, the research project. They provide an opportunity for the student to explain the work, present and interpret the principal results, and respond to questions from examiners with different levels of familiarity with the research area.

The examination will be conducted by a panel of three examiners:

·      the project supervisor;

·      an examiner with expertise relevant to the project; and

·      a non-specialist examiner.

The examination will normally last approximately 20–30 minutes. At the beginning of the examination, the student will give a very brief presentation of approximately 5 minutes, summarising the project’s motivation, aims, methods, and principal results. The remainder of the examination will consist of questions from the panel.

Students are expected to demonstrate an understanding of the complete thesis, including material developed collaboratively or with guidance from the supervisor. 

Questions may address:

·      the motivation, aims, and scientific context of the project;

·      the student’s individual contribution to the work;

·      the theoretical, experimental, or computational methods used;

·      the reasons for important methodological or analytical decisions;

·      the interpretation, reliability, and limitations of the results;

·      the relationship between the results and the existing literature;

·      alternative interpretations or approaches;

·      possible improvements, extensions, or future directions; and

·      the communication of the project to both specialist and non-specialist audiences.
